source.title: Towards World Simulator: Crafting Physical Commonsense-Based Benchmark for Video Generation
source.authors: Fan-Qing Meng; Jiaqi Liao; Xin-Yu Tan; Wen-Qi Shao; Quan-Feng Lu; Kai-Peng Zhang; Yu Cheng; Dianqi Li; Yu Qiao; Ping Luo

record.tranche_reason: The study compares video-generation models of two sizes on physical-commonsense benchmark scores, extending a scale/performance comparison to video models. It does not test language-model held-out loss scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The study reports a CogVideoX 2B-versus-5B comparison on PhyGenBench and says scaling improves some results but does not resolve dynamic phenomena. Its other model scores are not scale-controlled comparisons. Cited language-model scaling laws are not results from this study.
record.test_reason: This is a physical-commonsense benchmark for text-to-video diffusion models. Its only scale result compares two CogVideoX sizes (2B vs 5B) on benchmark scores. It measures no pretraining loss and fits no power law, so V1–V5 and V7 are untouched. Two sizes of a video diffusion model cannot show that downstream performance improves predictably with scale (V6), and the comparison is not a language-model downstream evaluation. The 2B/5B pair also differ in output resolution (720×480 vs 640×360, Table 5) and possibly other training choices, so size is not isolated. The authors call scaling laws a 'proven-effective' method and cite Kaplan et al.; that is a cited claim, not their result. The comparison is recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that current T2V models score low on physical commonsense, best model Gen-3 at 0.51. Scaling CogVideoX from 2B to 5B fixes some static-scene issues but not dynamic phenomena, which they suggest may need curated synthetic training data. Prompt rewriting and VEnhancer also fail to solve the problems.
record.recipe_differences: This study evaluates video-generation benchmark scores across model sizes, not language-model held-out loss or compute-optimal parameter/token allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: The study reports that scaling gains differ by physical category: progress is limited in Mechanics, while qualitative improvements are described for some static phenomena.

fits_no_version.finding: CogVideoX 5B scores higher than 2B on PhyGenBench physical-commonsense alignment: average 0.39→0.45, Optics 0.43→0.55, Mechanics 0.38→0.39. The authors say both sizes fail on dynamic phenomena such as a bouncing football.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Scaling text-to-video models improves benchmark physical-commonsense scores for static phenomena but not for dynamic mechanics.

record.problems: The scale comparison uses only two CogVideoX sizes, so it cannot establish a scaling curve or predictability. No uncertainty estimates are reported for the listed scores.
record.rows_left_out: Other models' Table 2 scores are not extracted because the paper does not present them as a controlled size sweep. Qualitative examples in Figure 7 are summarized in gate_note and authors_conclusion rather than duplicated as score rows.

untested.parts: No pretraining loss or power-law fit.
No shape comparison at fixed parameter count.
Video models are studied, but no power-law form is measured.
No scaling curve, predictability test or relation to loss; only two model sizes are compared.
No exponents or fitting choices examined.

record.verdict_notes: The study is primarily a benchmark and evaluator paper (PhyGenBench/PhyGenEval); scaling appears only in Appendix D. Model sizes across families (860M Lavie, 1.1B Open-Sora, 2B Vchitect) are not a controlled sweep. The reader's V6 'supports' label is dropped because two confounded sizes of a video model cannot show predictable scaling. The reader's 'partial' states on the 2B baseline rows were meaningless and are reset.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out language-model pretraining loss or power-law relationship in parameters, tokens, or compute is measured.
No power-law fit or extrapolation from smaller to larger runs is evaluated.
No fixed-compute allocation between parameters and tokens is evaluated.
No architecture comparison at fixed parameter count is reported.
Although the study concerns video models and compares two sizes, it does not measure whether a power-law form holds in video generation or any other modality or training regime.
The study compares benchmark performance for only two CogVideoX sizes; it does not fit or assess a predictable scaling curve, or relate performance to pretraining loss.
No fitted exponents, compute-optimal splits, or sensitivity to fitting choices are examined.
